src/articles/relational-collection/r01.a.text: This article develops the shop from the introduction, using its three customers, three orders and five order lines. We will compare those tables with a sales sheet that keeps the same purchases in a different shape.

In this alternative definition, the primary key gives other tables one value to reference; the unique pair preserves the meaning of an order line. Generating an identity value and enforcing uniqueness are separate jobs in PostgreSQL too: GENERATED … AS IDENTITY alone is not a unique constraint.
Figure 2 compares the sales sheet with separate customers and orders. Choose each change and compare where it has to go in the two designs. The rows below show why.

The mug has two prices: products.price and order_items.unit_price. At the time of order 103, they both say 20.00. Deleting the line price and looking up the catalogue price would seem to remove duplication, until the catalogue changes.
On 21 October 2026 at 09:00 UTC, the shop changes P7’s catalogue price to 25.00. Order 103 was placed the previous day. Follow the two values through that change.

A stored order total is different again. In this shop, the total is derived from the lines: order 103 is 1 × 20.00 + 2 × 4.50 = 29.00. The shop calculates it rather than storing an authoritative orders.total. A view can package that calculation for callers while the lines remain its source.

src/articles/relational-collection/r02.a.text: The shop’s order 103 gives us the amounts and times to start from. The examples use PostgreSQL 18. Later, optional delivery notes on the same three orders let us compare missing and empty text. The controls illustrate the logic; the accompanying SQL was checked on a disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 instance.

An integer number of minor units is another exact representation. With a scale of two decimal places, 4.50 becomes 450 and 20.00 becomes 2000: each integer counts hundredths of one unit. This works only with an agreed scale and adequate integer range. The shop’s example prices have no assigned currency. A real system handling several currencies must retain which currency an amount belongs to and apply its rounding rules; the integer 450 alone says neither.

The difference matters when the shop also sells tea classes. Its Tea tasting session S501 starts at 2026-11-04 18:00:00Z, with Europe/Stockholm as its display zone. Z means UTC, the common reference for instants. Follow the same start time through the two clocks.

The upper bound belongs to the next day, so it cannot be counted in both days. BETWEEN includes both endpoints and would include that next midnight. Avoid converting an event to a date without saying which zone defines the date. The shop’s three orders are all earlier, so this particular query returns no rows.
For the next example, give each order an optional delivery_note. Order 101 has 'Leave by door', order 102 has '', an empty string, and order 103 has NULL.
Start with note = '' in the figure, then choose note <> ''. Compare the answer and order 103’s condition result. Finally choose note IS NULL.

This is different from storing a payment whose amount is unknown. An unknown amount must not quietly become a zero payment. The shop requires every payment amount, and Aggregates, windows and ordered results follows how missing inputs affect counts, sums and averages.
